summary: Defines MIME, which lets email carry multi-part messages and non-text content such as images without losing information. It is based on RFC 934 and RFC 1049, extending and revising that earlier work. It was replaced by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048, RFC 2049.

plainLanguage.summary: Early email could only carry plain letters. MIME is like a box with labeled compartments so you can mail pictures and sounds too.

questions: what is base64 encoding in email
subtitle: How Internet email learned to carry attachments, images and non-ASCII text without breaking the old message format.

tldr.problem: RFC 822 mail was limited to short lines of seven-bit ASCII text, so images, audio, other languages and multi-part messages could not be sent without ad hoc conversion.
tldr.mechanism: MIME adds header fields (MIME-Version, Content-Type, Content-Transfer-Encoding, Content-ID, Content-Description) that label the body, plus seven content types, multipart bodies and two encodings that turn arbitrary data into mail-safe ASCII.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1521 revised RFC 1341 and was itself obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049, which split MIME into several parts.

today: RFC 1521 is a Draft Standard that has been obsoleted by RFC 2045, RFC 2046, RFC 2047, RFC 2048 and RFC 2049, and updated by RFC 1590. It obsoleted RFC 1341.

sections.title: Why Email Needed MIME
sections.content:
RFC 822 defined the format of Internet text messages, but it left the message body as flat ASCII text. Mail systems limited messages to relatively short lines of seven-bit ASCII, so anyone sending other data had to convert it first. The RFC lists encodings in use at the time, such as hexadecimal, uuencode and the base 64 scheme from RFC 1421.

Text in character sets richer than US-ASCII was also not covered. Gateways to X.400 systems had to either convert non-text body parts to ASCII or discard them, which loses information.

This document, written as a revision of RFC 1341, describes mechanisms that solve most of these problems without introducing any serious incompatibilities with existing RFC 822 mail. It is largely orthogonal to RFC 822 rather than a revision of it. It does not extend mail header fields to hold anything other than US-ASCII, which is left to a companion document, RFC 1522.
sections.plainLanguage: The old mail system only understood simple typed letters. People who wanted to send pictures had to disguise them as letters, and sometimes the pictures got lost.

sections.title: The MIME Header Fields
sections.content:
MIME works by adding labels in the message header. The MIME-Version field declares that the message follows this specification. Messages composed in accordance with it MUST include the verbatim text MIME-Version: 1.0. It is required at the top level of a message but not for each body part.

The Content-Type field describes the data in the body in a type/subtype form with optional parameters, for example text/plain; charset=us-ascii. The subtype is mandatory, and type, subtype and parameter names are case-insensitive. If no Content-Type is given, the default is plain text in US-ASCII. A reader meeting an unknown type should generally treat it as application/octet-stream.

Two more optional fields, Content-ID and Content-Description, further describe the body. New non-standard values must start with X-, or be registered with IANA.
sections.plainLanguage: MIME puts a sticker on the box saying what is inside, such as a picture or a song, so the receiver knows which tool to open it with.

sections.title: Content-Transfer-Encoding
sections.content:
Many useful types are naturally 8-bit or binary data, which some mail transports cannot carry. The Content-Transfer-Encoding field names an invertible mapping from the original data to a form that survives 7-bit transport. The values are 7bit (the default), 8bit, binary, quoted-printable and base64. The first three mean no encoding was performed; they only label what the data looks like. The RFC notes that there are no circumstances where binary is actually legal on the Internet transports of the time.

Quoted-printable is the readable encoding for mostly-ASCII text. A byte can be written as = followed by two hex digits, so an equals sign becomes =3D. Encoded lines must be no longer than 76 characters, with a trailing = marking a soft line break.

Base64 is the dense encoding for arbitrary data. It turns each group of 3 bytes into 4 characters from a 65-character subset of US-ASCII, so the result is about 33 percent larger. The RFC prefers base64 over quoted-printable for binary data.
sections.plainLanguage: Some mail pipes can only carry plain letters. These tricks rewrite pictures and other things into plain letters, then the other side turns them back, like writing a drawing out as a list of colored squares.

sections.title: The Seven Content Types and Multipart Messages
sections.content:
The RFC defines seven top-level types: text, multipart, message, image, audio, video and application. New types are meant to come mostly as new subtypes. Initial subtypes include text/plain, image/jpeg and image/gif, audio/basic, video/mpeg and application/octet-stream for uninterpreted binary data.

The multipart type combines several body parts in one message. It needs a boundary parameter of 1 to 70 characters. Each part starts after a line that is two hyphens plus the boundary, and the last boundary has two extra hyphens at the end. Parts can be nested. The subtypes are:

  • mixed: independent parts in order.
  • alternative: the same information in several formats, plainest first and richest last. A reader should show the last one it can display.
  • parallel: parts to be viewed at the same time.
  • digest: each part is a message.

The message type carries another message. message/partial splits a large message across several mails with id, number and total parameters, much like IP fragmentation. message/external-body points to data held elsewhere.
sections.plainLanguage: A multipart message is a box with dividers. Each compartment has its own label, and a special line tells you where one compartment ends and the next begins.

sections.title: Security and Conformance
sections.content:
The security section is brief. It points to the discussion of application/PostScript as a model for any content type that can cause remote execution of actions on the recipient's side. That section warns that running general-purpose PostScript interpreters entails serious security risks and names dangerous file operators such as deletefile and renamefile.

Appendix A defines minimal MIME conformance. A conforming mail user agent MUST always generate MIME-Version: 1.0, decode quoted-printable and base64, interpret Content-Type, and avoid showing users raw data that is not text. It must handle text, message, multipart and other types to at least the stated extents.
sections.plainLanguage: Some attachments can carry little programs that do things on your computer, so mail readers must be careful before running anything. The RFC also lists the minimum a mail program must do to count as MIME-ready.

data.title: multipart/mixed with two parts
data.code:
MIME-Version: 1.0
Content-type: multipart/mixed; boundary="simple
 boundary"

This is the preamble.  It is to be ignored.

--simple boundary

This is implicitly typed plain ASCII text.
It does NOT end with a linebreak.
--simple boundary
Content-type: text/plain; charset=us-ascii

This is explicitly typed plain ASCII text.
It DOES end with a linebreak.

--simple boundary--

This is the epilogue.  It is also to be ignored.

items.label: Default
items.desc: Short lines of US-ASCII data; no encoding performed.

items.label: Short lines, 8-bit
items.desc: Lines are short but may contain non-ASCII octets; no encoding performed.

items.label: Unrestricted
items.desc: Non-ASCII data and lines of any length; no encoding performed.

items.label: Readable encoding
items.desc: For mostly-ASCII text; non-printable octets written as = and two hex digits.

items.label: Dense encoding
items.desc: For arbitrary data; 3 bytes become 4 characters.
